title: Mathlib Imports and Namespace
content: A single `import Mathlib` pulls in the entire library, then `open Set Function` brings set-theoretic and function notations into scope. The file works inside the `Erdos477` namespace to avoid name collisions.

title: Polynomial Image
content: polyImage f is simply the range of $f : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$. For a polynomial $f$ of degree $d \geq 2$, this is a sparse subset of $\mathbb{Z}$: only $O(N^{1/d})$ elements lie in $[-N, N]$.

title: Perfect Complement
content: IsPerfectComplement A B holds when every integer $z$ has a *unique* representation $z = a + b$ with $a \in A$, $b \in B$. This is equivalent to saying $\mathbb{Z} = A \oplus B$ as a direct sum of sets under addition. The uniqueness condition is what makes this a tiling rather than just a covering.
mathContext: $\mathbb{Z} = A \oplus B \iff \forall z \in \mathbb{Z},\; \exists! (a,b) \in A \times B:\; a + b = z$

title: Non-emptiness of Complements
content: Two short proofs that both $A$ and $B$ must be non-empty in any perfect complement pair. If either were empty, no integer $z$ could be represented as $a + b$. These are proved by extracting witnesses from the representation of $z = 0$.

title: Singleton Complement Characterization
content: If $A = \{0\}$, then $A \oplus B = \mathbb{Z}$ iff $B = \mathbb{Z}$. This is the trivial case: shifting by 0 doesn't help. The proof uses extensionality in both directions.

title: Linear Case is Trivial
content: For $f(x) = x$ (degree 1), $A = \{0\}$ is a perfect complement since $f(\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}$. This demonstrates why Erdős requires degree $\geq 2$: the problem is trivial for linear polynomials.

title: Covering and Uniqueness Properties
content: Two structural lemmas: (1) every $z$ is covered by some $a + b$, and (2) representations are unique. These factor the perfect complement definition into its two components and are used as building blocks throughout.

title: Commutativity and Shift Invariance
content: Perfect complements are commutative ($A \oplus B = \mathbb{Z} \implies B \oplus A = \mathbb{Z}$) and invariant under opposite shifts ($A + c$ and $B - c$ remain a perfect complement). These symmetries show the problem is about the 'shape' of the sets, not their position.
mathContext: $A \oplus B = \mathbb{Z} \iff B \oplus A = \mathbb{Z}$; also $(A + c) \oplus (B - c) = \mathbb{Z}$

title: Properties of Polynomial Images
content: Basic properties: $f(0) \in f(\mathbb{Z})$, injective polynomials have infinite images, the image of $x^2$ is non-negative, and negative integers are not squares. These establish the structural constraints on $B = f(\mathbb{Z})$ that make complementation difficult.

title: Difference Set Constraint
content: The key structural theorem: if $A \oplus B = \mathbb{Z}$, then $(A - A) \cap (B - B) = \{0\}$. The only difference appearing in both $A$ and $B$ is zero. This follows because $a_1 - a_2 = b_2 - b_1$ implies $a_1 + b_1 = a_2 + b_2$, contradicting uniqueness unless $a_1 = a_2$. This constraint severely restricts which sets can tile.

title: No Complement with Finite B
content: If $B$ is finite and non-empty, then $A$ must be infinite in any perfect complement pair. The proof: if both are finite, $A + B$ is finite, but $\mathbb{Z}$ is infinite. This is why polynomial images (infinite but sparse) are the interesting case.

title: Structural Analysis for Squares
content: Several lemmas analyzing $f(x) = x^2$: the complement must contain elements representing all negative integers (since squares are non-negative), $0, 1, 4 \in f(\mathbb{Z})$ explicitly, and between consecutive squares $n^2$ and $(n+1)^2$ there are $2n+1$ gaps that $A$ must fill. This gap-filling becomes increasingly constrained.
mathContext: $(n+1)^2 - n^2 = 2n+1$; all $z < 0$ need $a \in A$ with $a + n^2 = z$

title: Erdős Problem 477 (Open)
content: The main conjecture in three forms: (1) no degree $\geq 2$ polynomial has a perfect complement, (2) no monomial $x^k$ with $k \geq 2$ has a perfect complement, and (3) the combined statement. The formalization also notes connections to the Coven-Meyerowitz conjecture on integer tilings.
